title: Universal neurons in gpt2 language models
contribution: A student-led empirical study, on which Bertsimas is a co-senior author who 'supported the project and edited the paper', finding that only 1-5% of GPT2 neurons are universal across five random seeds and that these neurons are mostly interpretable, fall into a few families and include prediction, suppression, entropy and attention-deactivation neurons.
problem_entry: ML (mechanistic interpretability; outside the council's optimization scope, no optimization model): are neural mechanisms universal across models (abstract, p. 1)? Motivated by LLMs deployed 'in high-stakes settings' and by Olah et al.'s universality hypothesis read as a discovery strategy and a triage rule for the field (p. 1); five seeds of one architecture as the smallest variation, to bound universality under larger changes (pp. 2, 4).
key_idea: Universality as an unsupervised filter: excess correlation = mean over seeds of the max activation correlation minus the same max against a random Gaussian rotation of the layer (eqs. 2-3, p. 4); study neurons with excess correlation > 0.5 (p. 5), label families with several hundred automated variance-reduction tests (p. 6), and read functional roles from weights (prediction/suppression/partition, entropy via LayerNorm, attention deactivation via BOS; pp. 7-10).
assumptions: GPT2-small and GPT2-medium replications, five seeds each, plus Pythia-160m and Pythia 410M-6.9B (pp. 4-5, 8, 18); 100M Pile test tokens at context 512 without padding, BOS and newline tokens (p. 18); weights preprocessed so cosines have mean 0 (p. 18); a seed change taken as 'the smallest change' (p. 4); the 0.5 threshold admittedly unprincipled (p. 5); labels from vocabulary, spaCy, Pile subsets and an SVD topic model, leaving many neurons uncategorized (pp. 6-7).
proof_devices: n/a for proofs, reformulations or bounds (empirical work); random-rotation baseline (a random Gaussian matrix applied to a layer's activations) to test whether the neuron basis is privileged (p. 4)
Excess correlation: mean over models of the max correlation minus the max baseline correlation (eq. 3, p. 4)
Variance-reduction score of a binary explanation, 1 - ((1-beta) var(v|y=0) + beta var(v|y=1)) / var(v), over several hundred automated tests (eq. 4, p. 6)
Moment signature of the vocabulary-effect vector W_U w_out: high kurtosis with positive skew = prediction, negative skew = suppression, high variance = partition (pp. 7-8)
Causal intervention fixing one neuron's activation, against 20 random neurons from the last two layers outside the top norm decile and bottom logit-variance decile (p. 9)
Heuristic score h_n = W_out^T W_Q^T k_BOS checked by zero path ablation (p. 10)
Streaming all-pairs correlation from running sums instead of storing 36 PB of activations (p. 18)
experiments: 1,253 of 98,304 GPT2-medium-a neurons with excess correlation > 0.5; shares 1.23% (GPT2-medium), 1.26% (Pythia-160M), 4.16% (GPT2-small, unexplained outlier) (pp. 5, 11-12); families incl. alphabet neurons for 18 of 26 letters (p. 6); prediction/suppression depth pattern consistent across seeds and repeated on Pythia 410M-6.9B (p. 8); entropy/anti-entropy pair with cosine -0.886 (p. 9); baselines: random rotation, random neurons, random directions (pp. 4, 9, 10); unexplained results in 'Additional Mysteries' and an entropy-neuron counter-case printed (pp. 10-12); code and data released (p. 18). No solver, benchmark or decision metric.
positioning: Builds on Olah et al. 2020b's universality hypothesis and the circuits programme (p. 1); representational-similarity work has 'yielded mixed conclusions' (p. 3); follows Voita et al. 2023 for position neurons (pp. 6-7); refines Geva et al. 2022 from promoting to promoting and suppressing (p. 8); claims the first documented uncertainty mechanism in language models (p. 10); cites the group's 2023 sparse-probing preprint (p. 15); no optimization or OR work cited (pp. 13-17).
writing: Abstract: question, method with numbers, families, three functional roles (p. 1); Figure 1 as a visual abstract (p. 2); hypothesis-first, heavily hedged prose ('We intuit', p. 8; 'speculations', p. 5) in an informal register (p. 6); a separate 'Additional Mysteries' section (p. 11); concrete limitations and future work (pp. 12-13); a role-by-initials author contribution statement (p. 13).
limits_future: Empirical-science contribution with released analysis code (pp. 12, 18). Limits stated specifically: small models (hundreds of millions of parameters), seed-only universality within one family, tokenization blocks cross-family study, all-pairs correlation cost, manual or algorithmic supervision, neuron basis ignores most computation (pp. 12-13). Future: overcomplete dictionary basis, adjacent-layer correlations for larger models, LLM-generated explanations, training dynamics and circuits (p. 13).

method_links.note: A student-carried line with five other MIT authors (p. 1), continuing the group's 2023 preprint (p. 15), fits programme steps 2-3; but the hands-on method partner is a co-senior author from outside optimization ('NN gave frequent and detailed feedback on experiment design and analysis', p. 13), unlike the close-network co-advisers of step 3 [inferred], and his own part is stated as support and editing (p. 13); none of his methods appears: a programme he sponsors rather than shapes. Not counted: Heuristic 8 evidence (second adviser carries method feedback, p. 13); Taste mark 5 consistent (high-stakes interpretability, p. 1); Methods 1-5 not engaged, not counter-evidence given his stated role.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: sponsor-and-edit senior authorship on student-led lines outside optimization
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Two senior authors marked (p. 1); 'WG led the project, conducted most of the analysis, and wrote most of the paper'; NN gave feedback on experiment design and analysis; 'DB supported the project and edited the paper' (p. 13); no optimization content anywhere (pp. 1-18).

transferable: Test whether coordinates carry meaning with a random-rotation null: recompute the statistic after multiplying the layer by a random Gaussian matrix and report only the excess over that baseline (eqs. 2-3, p. 4).
Compute all pairwise correlations over 10^8 samples from running sums (means, sums of squares, cross-products) instead of storing the data (p. 18).
Auto-label units with a variance-reduction score for each binary candidate explanation, over hundreds of programmatic labels (eq. 4, p. 6).
Classify effect vectors by moments: kurtosis for concentration, sign of skew for promote vs suppress, variance for partition (pp. 7-8).

Intervene on a selected unit against a matched random control set that excludes the extremes of the selection criteria (p. 9), and repeat on a second model family to rule out an architectural artifact (p. 8).
Report unexplained observations in a section of their own and close with a role-by-initials contribution statement (pp. 11, 13).
coauthors: Wes Gurnee (MIT, lead), Theo Horsley (Cambridge), Zifan Carl Guo, Tara Rezaei Kheirkhah, Qinyi Sun, Will Hathaway (MIT), Neel Nanda (co-senior author)

quotes.text: Taken seriously, these hypotheses suggest a strategy for discovering important features and circuits: look for that which is universal.
DB supported the project and edited the paper.

title: Robust and adaptive optimization under a large language model lens
contribution: A prompting demonstration, with his PhD student Margaritis, that ChatGPT 3.5 given his book's reformulation rules as step-wise context prompts can formulate simple LO problems, add user-specified uncertainty, derive robust and linear-decision-rule adaptive counterparts and write JuMP/Gurobi code, shown by curated transcripts with failure examples and no quantitative evaluation.
problem_entry: RO+ML: an adoption gap, not a tractability gap: optimization needs modelling experts while ML packages need 'just a few lines of code' (pp. 1-2); RO and ARO need still more expertise (pp. 2-3); ChatGPT asserted to perform 'very poorly out-of-the-box' (p. 4, not measured); can prompting automate formulate, robustify, counterpart and code (abstract, p. 1; pp. 3-4)?
key_idea: A four-step chain of thought (nominal LO, uncertain parameters, robust counterpart, Julia/JuMP/Gurobi code) with context prompts only for steps 2-4 that carry the book's rules: robustification template, closed-form or support-function counterparts with intersection and Minkowski rules, l1/linf linearization and SOC for l2, ARO with a linear decision rule (pp. 8-11, 21-23); targets the theorem-application step that NL4Opt-type work does not (pp. 3-4).
assumptions: LO with (c, A, b) in a user-specified set, reduced to row-wise uncertainty in a_i (pp. 5-6); p-norm, polyhedral, intersection, Minkowski and entropy-type sets (pp. 7, 10); ARO with fixed recourse, constant RHS and an LDR, admitted as an approximation 'necessary to make the problem tractable' (p. 20); small toy instances with r = 0.1 in the first code (pp. 11-30, 13); ChatGPT 3.5 (p. 4); number of runs, sampling settings and transcript selection not stated, responses cut (p. 11).
proof_devices: No new theorem, bound or algorithm; devices of Bertsimas and den Hertog (2022) restated as a teaching sequence (pp. 5-7, 20-21)
Epigraph moves objective uncertainty into the constraints; row-wise projection U_i and absorption of an uncertain b (eq. 3, pp. 5-6)
Support-function robust counterpart a^T x + delta*(P^T x | Z) <= b (eqs. 7-9, pp. 6-7)
Dual-norm counterparts for p-norm balls and LP duality for polyhedral sets (eqs. 11-13, p. 7)
Intersection of sets handled by splitting P^T x into a sum of w^i (eqs. 14-15, p. 7)
Linear decision rule y(z) = u + V^T z turns a fixed-recourse ARO constraint into a static robust one (eqs. 17-20, pp. 20-21)
Linearization of l1 and linf terms and an SOC for l2 as the solver-facing step (Prompt 2.4, p. 11)
experiments: Curated transcripts judged by author inspection: RO examples (pp. 11-19), ARO examples (pp. 23-27), failure cases: run-to-run inconsistency, a = [-99, 1] instead of [-99, -1], intersection treated as a Minkowski sum (pp. 28-31); no trial counts, success rates, test set, baseline or solver output. [my reading] RO Example 1's printed counterpart swaps the 2-norm and 1-norm between the two constraints (pp. 9, 11-14) yet is presented as correct; [my computation] the diet code has no radius r and is infeasible as printed (SciPy HiGHS: min cost 110 vs budget 50) though the text says it 'solves the problem with example data' (pp. 17-19).
positioning: Related work: NL4Opt (Ramamonjison et al. 2023), a BERT/BART pipeline (Ramamonjison et al. 2022), a position paper (Tsouros et al. 2023) (p. 3); claims to be the first approach for RO/ARO (p. 4); RO background from his own book with den Hertog and the SIAM Review survey (pp. 2, 5-7, 20); no RO modelling software or other non-LLM route to counterparts cited (pp. 32-33).
writing: Abstract: capabilities (i)-(iv), 'little to no errors', then 'some instances of erroneous execution' (p. 1); 'two-fold' contribution (p. 4); tutorial 'Let's' voice (pp. 6-7, 20); commentary lists challenges overcome (pp. 14, 19, 24); failures confined to Limitations (pp. 27-31); results 'surprising' and the ML-packages analogy close the paper (pp. 31-32); title reuses the under-a-lens programme brand (p. 1); typos and notation slips mark an early draft (pp. 1-3, 7, 20).
limits_future: Demonstration-level contribution (p. 4). Limits stated with examples: inconsistency across runs, algebraic manipulation, choosing and applying theorems (pp. 28-31), attributed to 'inherent weaknesses of Large Language Models' (p. 31). Future: LLMs as a learning resource and formulation aid for non-experts, raising the field's visibility (pp. 31-32); no benchmark, tool or experiment proposed. [my reading] 'little to no errors' (p. 1) rests on showcased transcripts that contain unremarked problems (pp. 13-19).

method_links.note: The prompts teach Method 1's class-keeping toolkit (dual norms, LP duality for polyhedra, linearized l1/linf, a cone for l2; a linear decision rule keeping ARO a static robust problem, approximation admitted, p. 20) so that the counterpart 'can be solved by traditional optimizers efficiently' (p. 3); evidence of the toolkit as he teaches it, not of new formulation work.

The skill cites this paper for step 6 (return when a tool changes): the return holds (ChatGPT 3.5 with in-context learning, pp. 3-4), but the reopened belief concerns accessibility, not intractability (pp. 1-3), nothing is conceded as once right, and the why-now is unquantified: out-of-the-box failure asserted, not measured (p. 4); no success rate for the prompted version (pp. 11-31).

Outside the method's IO/ML home: no duel against any incumbent (out-of-the-box, human or software), no certificate that a counterpart is correct, no solver status for generated code; the headline 'little to no errors' (p. 1) rests on author inspection, which did not flag a swapped-norm counterpart (pp. 9, 11-14), and the text says the diet code 'solves the problem with example data' (p. 19) for an instance infeasible as printed (my computation, pp. 17-19).

Stated purpose is teaching and adoption: a learning resource and formulation aid for non-experts, widening the field as ML packages did (pp. 31-32); the book's rules become the prompts (book to tool, pp. 5-7, 20); the co-author is his PhD student (ORC, p. 1). Supports the skill's inference that recent research follows his education role. Not counted: Heuristic 9 evidence (brand in the title, p. 1); Tension T6 headline vs caveat (pp. 1, 13-19, 27-31); Methods 3 and 5 not engaged (r fixed at 0.1 or absent, no price curve; no owner or decision metric).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Every rule in Prompts 2.1-2.6 restates Bertsimas and den Hertog (2022): robustification template, closed-form and support-function counterparts, combination rules, linearization, LDR counterpart; the LLM is tested on the steps an expert would perform (pp. 5-11, 20-23).

Optimization is less popular than ML because it needs modelling experts while ML packages need a few lines of code (pp. 1-2); the aim is LLMs as a learning resource and formulation aid for non-experts that make the field more popular (pp. 31-32).

Success transcripts followed by commentary on challenges overcome (pp. 14, 19, 24), failures in a separate Limitations section (pp. 27-31), responses cut (p. 11), no counts, rates or baseline (pp. 11-31).

transferable: Split an expert reformulation into stages (nominal model, uncertainty, counterpart, code) and give the LLM rule prompts only for the stages it cannot already do (p. 8).
Prepare two tiers of rule prompts, closed forms per set and a general support-function calculus with combination rules, and test whether the model can use the general one (pp. 9-10, 19).
Probe extrapolation by asking for a construct the prompts never describe (a quadratic decision rule after only linear ones, p. 24), and probe robustness by merging two steps into one prompt (p. 19).
Organize failures by type with one minimal reproducible transcript each: run-to-run inconsistency, algebraic rearrangement, wrong theorem (pp. 28-31).
Teach robust counterparts in this order: epigraph, row-wise projection, support function, closed forms per set, combination rules, then linearization and cones for the solver (pp. 5-7, 11).

[critic-informed, from this card's checks; not the paper's practice] Check every generated counterpart mechanically against a reference counterpart and run every generated program, reporting solver status; here inspection let a swapped norm and an infeasible instance through (pp. 13-19).
coauthors: Georgios Margaritis (Operations Research Center, MIT; his PhD student)

quotes.text: For simple Optimization Problems, we show that ChatGPT is able to perform these steps with little to no errors.
LLMs that have been adapted to such specialized Optimization fields can (i) act as a helpful learning resource for non-experts
